government.name: Town of Comox
government.howBuilt: This list draws on 2026 local news coverage of the Comox Official Community Plan vote, contested housing proposals, the 2026 budget and tax debate, council discussion of CFB Comox growth, the new tree protection bylaw, and candidates' own campaign announcements. We kept issues the Town of Comox can act on through zoning, its budget, bylaws, streets, parks and recreation. Provincial matters such as health care and doctor recruitment are left out of this list.

issues.title: Housing growth and density
issues.description: How much new housing Comox allows, how dense and tall it can be, and where it goes under the new Official Community Plan.
issues.whatItAffects: Renters, buyers, families, workers arriving with the CFB Comox expansion, and neighbours of new projects.
issues.whoDecides: Council adopts the Official Community Plan and zoning, and approves or rejects rezonings and development permits.

viewQuestion.question: How should Comox approach new housing?
viewQuestion.poleA: Allow more homes and higher density where the plan permits
viewQuestion.poleB: Grow more gradually with lower density near existing homes

tradeoffs.context: Housing choices often trade how quickly new homes are built against how much existing neighbourhoods change.

gains: More homes could be built sooner for new and current residents
Compact growth may support transit, shops and walkable streets
costs: Neighbours may see more traffic, height and loss of trees
Pipes, roads and parks may need upgrades sooner

gains: Existing neighbourhoods may keep their current scale and feel
Growth may be easier to match with roads and services
costs: Fewer new homes could keep rents and prices higher
Some housing demand may shift to outlying areas, adding car trips

issues.title: Property taxes and town spending
issues.description: How much property taxes rise each year and what the town spends on services, projects and infrastructure renewal.
issues.whatItAffects: Homeowners, renters through their rents, businesses, and everyone who uses town services.
issues.whoDecides: Council adopts the five-year financial plan and sets municipal tax rates and the infrastructure renewal levy.

viewQuestion.question: What should guide the town budget?
viewQuestion.poleA: Keep tax increases low, even if some projects wait
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep funding services and projects, even if taxes rise more

tradeoffs.context: With limited revenue, lower tax increases usually mean doing less or doing it later.

gains: Households and businesses could face smaller yearly tax bills
Council may look harder for savings in existing programs
costs: Some projects or service improvements could be delayed
Deferred maintenance can cost more to fix later

gains: Services and planned projects may continue on schedule
Infrastructure could be renewed before it wears out
costs: Property tax bills could rise faster
Higher costs may add to pressure on renters and fixed incomes

issues.title: Infrastructure for growth
issues.description: How the town pays for roads, water, sewer and other services needed as Comox grows, including growth tied to the CFB Comox expansion.
issues.whatItAffects: Residents who rely on town water, sewer and roads, developers, and future taxpayers.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets development cost charges and amenity contributions, plans capital projects and decides how much to borrow or levy.

viewQuestion.question: Who should pay most of the cost of growth-related upgrades?
viewQuestion.poleA: New development, through higher charges on builders
viewQuestion.poleB: The whole community, keeping development charges moderate

tradeoffs.context: Upgrades for growth have to be paid for either by new development or by existing taxpayers.

gains: Existing taxpayers may carry less of the cost of growth
Upgrades could be funded as new projects arrive
costs: Higher charges could raise the price of new homes
Some projects may be delayed or not built

gains: Lower charges may help more housing get built
Costs are spread across all who benefit over time
costs: Existing taxpayers may pay more for upgrades
Upgrades could lag if tax revenue falls short

issues.title: Traffic and getting around
issues.description: How Comox streets handle growing traffic and how space is shared among cars, parking, walking, cycling and buses.
issues.whatItAffects: Drivers, cyclists, pedestrians, transit riders, and residents on busy streets.
issues.whoDecides: Council funds street design, traffic calming, bike lanes, sidewalks and trails, and works with regional partners on transit.

viewQuestion.question: How should street space be used as Comox grows?
viewQuestion.poleA: Give more space to walking, cycling and transit
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep more space for driving lanes and parking

tradeoffs.context: Street space is fixed, so adding room for one way of travel often takes it from another.

gains: Walking and cycling could become safer and more appealing
More trips by foot, bike or bus may ease future congestion
costs: Some on-street parking and driving lanes may be lost
Changes can be costly and take years to show results

gains: Drivers and businesses may keep familiar parking and access
Fewer construction projects may be needed in the short term
costs: Congestion may grow as population rises
People who do not drive may have fewer safe options

issues.title: Parks, trees and environment
issues.description: How the town protects trees, green space and shorelines and prepares for climate impacts such as drought.
issues.whatItAffects: Property owners, park users, wildlife habitat, and the town's water supply and climate readiness.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets the tree protection bylaw, buys and manages parkland, and funds climate and urban forest plans.

viewQuestion.question: How far should the town go to protect trees and green space?
viewQuestion.poleA: Stronger rules and more spending to protect trees and land
viewQuestion.poleB: Lighter rules for owners and less spending on new land

tradeoffs.context: Protecting trees and green space usually trades property owner flexibility and cost for long-term environmental benefits.

gains: More tree canopy, habitat and green space could be kept
The town may be better prepared for heat and drought
costs: Owners may face permits and replanting costs
Buying land and running programs adds to budgets

gains: Owners may have more freedom on their own property
Lower spending could ease pressure on taxes
costs: Tree canopy and green space may shrink as the town grows
Climate impacts may cost more to handle later

issues.title: Youth and recreation
issues.description: How much the town invests in recreation facilities and programs, especially for youth.
issues.whatItAffects: Young people, families, seniors and users of the community centre and parks.
issues.whoDecides: Council funds town recreation facilities and programs and sets fees through the budget and recreation master plan.

viewQuestion.question: How should the town approach recreation?
viewQuestion.poleA: Add facilities and low-cost programs, even at higher cost
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep spending steady and focus on existing facilities

tradeoffs.context: New recreation options bring community benefits but add building and operating costs.

gains: Youth and families could have more places to be active
Low-cost programs may reach people who cannot afford fees
costs: New facilities add long-term operating costs
Money may come from taxes or other priorities

gains: Spending and tax pressure may stay more predictable
Existing facilities may be better maintained
costs: Some groups may see few new options
Demand may outgrow facilities as the town grows

issues.title: Downtown and local economy
issues.description: Where the town focuses its economic development efforts, from downtown and the marina to industrial and employment lands.
issues.whatItAffects: Local businesses, workers, shoppers, visitors and the town's commercial tax base.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets economic development strategy, zoning for commercial and industrial land, and funds downtown and marina projects.

viewQuestion.question: Where should the town focus economic development?
viewQuestion.poleA: Invest in downtown, the marina and the waterfront
viewQuestion.poleB: Open up more industrial and employment land elsewhere

tradeoffs.context: Economic development dollars and staff time are limited, so focusing on one area means less for another.

gains: A livelier downtown and waterfront could draw visitors and shoppers
Public spaces may benefit residents too
costs: Upfront costs fall on taxpayers
Benefits may be concentrated in one part of town

gains: New businesses and jobs could broaden the tax base
Industrial land may support trades tied to growth
costs: Servicing new employment land can be costly
Downtown may see less direct investment

issues.title: Public input on major decisions
issues.description: How much the town consults residents before major decisions such as rezonings, plans and large projects.
issues.whatItAffects: Residents near proposed projects, applicants waiting on approvals, and trust in local government.
issues.whoDecides: Council decides how much consultation to require beyond provincial rules, including public meetings, neighbourhood planning and citizens' assemblies.

viewQuestion.question: How should the town balance consultation and speed?
viewQuestion.poleA: Consult more widely, even if decisions take longer
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep processes streamlined so decisions move faster

tradeoffs.context: More consultation can improve buy-in but usually adds time and cost to decisions.

gains: Residents may feel more heard and trust outcomes more
Local knowledge could improve projects
costs: Approvals and housing could take longer
Consultation adds staff costs

gains: Projects and homes could be approved sooner
Applicants may face more predictable timelines
costs: Some residents may feel left out of decisions
Concerns may surface later, after approval

election.name: Town of Comox general local election
election.howToVote: On General Voting Day (Saturday, Oct. 17, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.) Comox voters cast ballots at the Comox Community Centre, 1855 Noel Avenue, or can vote early on any of four advance voting days. Voters already registered need no ID; others can register at the voting place with two pieces of ID (at least one with a signature) proving identity and residence. Non-resident property electors also need proof of ownership, such as a State of Title Certificate or current tax notice. Only the six council seats are contested; the mayor was acclaimed.
election.voteByMail: All eligible electors could apply to vote by mail; the application deadline was Sept. 25, 2026, and completed ballots must reach the Town by 8 p.m. on Oct. 17 (by mail or dropped off at Town Hall). Curbside voting is available on General Voting Day for voters with mobility challenges.

candidates.name: Nicole Minions
candidates.summary: Mayor of Comox since 2022 and a councillor from 2018. Background in banking, non-profit leadership, real estate and human resources; moved to the Comox Valley in 2012. Acclaimed to a second term as mayor.

positions.summary: Focuses on core services during economic pressure, favouring low-cost initiatives such as pop-ups and markets to do more with less.
Wants to continue momentum on downtown and marina improvements.
Said during OCP debate that balanced growth did not require the level of density in the adopted plan.
Lists environmental protection and climate action among her priorities.
Prioritizes closer partnership with 19 Wing Comox as the base expands.
positions.leanReason: No side on an issue scale

candidates.name: Steve Blacklock
candidates.summary: First elected to Comox council in 2022 after finishing second in a 2021 by-election; seeking a second term.

positions.summary: Lists managing town finances sustainably as Comox grows as a campaign priority.
Supports investing in infrastructure needed to support development.
Supports adding recreation facilities for residents.
Cites council's purchase of the Newson Family Park waterfront parcel as an accomplishment.
Lists economic development and support for business as a priority.

candidates.name: Ken Grant
candidates.summary: Long-serving incumbent Comox councillor seeking re-election.

positions.summary: Called repeated annual tax increases unreasonable and asked council to discuss changes at strategic planning.
Expects traffic to worsen with CFB Comox growth and says taxation and traffic should be council priorities.

candidates.name: Christopher Haslett
candidates.summary: Incumbent councillor first elected in 2022. Owns a Comox Valley yard maintenance business and has served on the Comox Valley Healthcare Foundation board (per 2022 profile).

candidates.name: Jonathan Kerr
candidates.summary: Family physician with a practice in downtown Comox and small business owner; first elected to council in 2022. Chairs the Comox Valley family physician recruitment and retention committee.

positions.summary: Voted against the adopted OCP, saying it should be a community plan rather than a developer plan.
positions.leanReason: Opposed the plan's approach to growth

positions.summary: Supports housing affordability initiatives, including the new regional Affordable Housing Authority.
Supports the Climate Action Plan and tree protection bylaw and protecting parks, forests and shorelines.
Supports funding recreation facilities for youth and seniors.
Prioritizes support for local businesses and downtown vitality.

candidates.name: Neil Ladell
candidates.summary: Federal public servant who has worked at Fisheries and Oceans Canada and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada; holds a PhD in resource and environmental management from SFU. First run for office.

positions.summary: Supports affordable, innovative housing while preserving Comox's community character.
Wants integrated planning for infrastructure, finances and climate pressures such as drought, plus sustainable urban forestry.
Wants stronger resident participation in decisions such as rezonings and infrastructure upgrades.
Lists youth recreation, arts, culture and inclusive gathering spaces among priorities.

candidates.name: Jenn Meilleur
candidates.summary: Has more than 20 years of experience in community development and sustainability in government and non-profits; completing her first term on Comox council.

positions.summary: Voted against the adopted OCP, wanting more consultation among developers, businesses and residents to resolve differing views.
Proposes neighbourhood planning and citizens' assemblies to widen democratic participation.
Supports managed growth paired with housing affordability.
Prioritizes ecosystem health, climate adaptation, and food and water security.
Prioritizes youth wellness and inclusive services for people with disabilities.

candidates.name: Ruby Sidhu
candidates.summary: Comox homeowner and father of two with a bachelor's degree in physics, mathematics and computer science; ran for Comox council in 2022 (per 2022 profile).

candidates.name: Maureen Swift
candidates.summary: Incumbent Comox councillor with experience in local government and community service; describes Comox as her long-term home.

positions.summary: Encourages development of industrial lands in Northeast Comox.
Encourages more housing options in Northeast Comox.
Supports expanding pedestrian and trail connections across the community.
Wants to improve recreation opportunities for young residents.
Says finances should be managed by weighing what the community wants against what it needs.

candidates.name: Jessica Wegg
candidates.summary: Lawyer licensed in Canada and the US and partner in her firm, with a master's in clinical psychology; past chair of the Brooklyn PAC. Has run federally twice; first municipal campaign.

positions.summary: Wants more safe, accessible and free recreation spaces for local teens.
Supports climate mitigation, emergency preparedness and environmental stewardship.
Pledges transparent tracking of town spending, prioritizing residents' interests over developer and corporate profits.
